item.title: Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9d84874dzjo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight - Published On 8 July, US President Donald Trump boarded Air Force One in plain sight of television cameras as he departed the Nato summit in Turkey. But when the mighty Boeing aircraft left Ankara, the president had reportedly already been secretly spirited away via a catering truck to a C-32A, a military version of the Boeing 757, which flew the president to RAF Mildenhall in the UK. Those left on board were unwitting decoys and had no indication that Trump was no longer travelling with them. But deception of this kind is not unusual. "That's very common," said Ronald Kessler, an author who has written extensively on the agency. "There's a long history of strategies to mislead anybody who might be trying to harm the president." Robert McDonald, a former high-ranking Secret Service agent with experience working on presidential security details, told the BBC that smaller-scale deceptions are used frequently during motorcade operations. These motorcades - which often include dozens of security and support vehicles, as well as ambulances and vans carrying White House reporters - typically include two "Beasts", as the enhanced limousine carrying the president is known. While one vehicle carries the president, the other travels nearby as a decoy, switching locations while en route to the destination. "It's what we call a shell game," said McDonald, who drove one of the vehicles during President George W Bush's administration. "Even in DC if we headed to Andrews [Joint Base Andrews - where Air Force One flies from], those two limousines would change position, like under a highway overpass." "But that would happen out of sight of anybody other than those in the motorcade or in that tunnel," he added. "Different things are used to mix up the bad guy." Similarly, Marine One - the president's helicopter - routinely flies in groups of three, changing positions so that potential threats are not sure which is carrying the US leader. Even more elaborate deceptions are carried out for complex, high-risk trips abroad. "I would say it does not happen often," former Secret Service agent Paul Eckloff told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme of the aircraft switch. "But it is an option that the Secret Service and others in executive protection always have." "When the president travels to war zones, there are frequently tactics and techniques used to create doubt in an adversary of which aircraft or which movement that he's going to make," he added. In March 2000, for example, then-President Bill Clinton flew from India to the Pakistani capital of Islamabad on an unmarked executive jet that landed after a decoy jet with all the livery of Air Force One. Three years later, the White House claimed that George W Bush would spend Thanksgiving in Texas, only to arrive in Baghdad in a blacked-out Air Force One. In 2023, Joe Biden also was secretly taken to Ukraine with a slimmed down press pool of one reporter and one photographer. In all three of those cases, the media on board was aware of the deception but had been asked to not report it in real time. The exact nature of the perceived threat to the aircraft in this latest case remains unclear. The Secret Service has so far not commented on the incident, while the White House has neither confirmed nor denied it, saying only that it uses every tool available to protect the president. While contingency plans for a variety of scenarios are developed ahead of time, experts say that the Secret Service needs to maintain flexibility and remain poised to improvise in the face of new threats as they emerge, particularly overseas. But according to McDonald, the extraordinary measure of secretly moving President Trump from the aircraft suggests that the potential danger was deemed, likely by multiple agencies, to be serious. "That tells me that the threat level in Turkey was relatively substantial and quite high," he said, adding that the president's staff, the Secret Service and the White House Military Office were almost certainly immediately alerted. "Those people likely got together in a room and were presented with this intelligence," McDonald explained. "And a plan was put together to negate the threat from whatever intelligence was received." McDonald's assessment was echoed by Marc Polymeropoulos, a 26-year veteran of the CIA who served in both Iraq and Afghanistan and oversaw clandestine missions around the world. "The key part of this is the nature of the threat, and what was so severe that the Secret Service would put forth such a deception operation," he said. A key question going forward, according to Polymeropoulos, is whether the government and intelligence community then had a duty to warn those on the aircraft. "Let's say the plane was blown out of the sky, and we knew about it," he said. "We don't do that…we can't. If we know ISIS is going to attack a target in Moscow, we warn the Russians. Why do we warn the Russians? Because if there's an American citizen killed in that, we can't let that happen." How much danger those who remained on the aircraft were in - or whether they were in danger at all - remains unclear. Journalists on board reported that they were repeatedly instructed to keep their window blinds down, a "not uncommon" practice McDonald said shows that steps were still being taken to protect the passengers. "A large plane flying overhead where somebody could see it, with the shades up and windows illuminated, could tell somebody that it's a particular type of aircraft," he said. "I appreciate the need for transparency, but [the passengers] are also part of the roadshow. We've got to make sure that you and everybody gets home safe." The Secret Service, he added, is under no legal obligation to inform of potential threats or detail operations being carried out to protect the president and his entourage. That decision would need to be made by the White House or other agencies. "The Secret Service is not in the business of public relations," he said. "We're very good at keeping secrets, as our name says. Everybody doesn't need to know everything." Related topics - Published2 hours ago

item.title: Anguish of Colombian brother at rubble of building being searched for earthquake survivors
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxerlglgw5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Anguish of Colombian brother at rubble of building being searched for earthquake survivors - Published Efraín Gallego does not lose faith that his brother will be found alive, although when he speaks about him, trapped beneath the rubble of a building, his voice breaks and he swallows hard until he regains his composure. "You feel anguish. Every time there is an alert about someone being alive, hope is reborn that we will find him," Gallego tells me emotionally. His 80-year-old brother was buried along with his wife when the Torres del Limonar building collapsed in Cali. This city in south-western Colombia is one of the hardest hit by the earthquake. The building has become a symbol of the tragedy in the country's third most populous city. Cali has more than two million inhabitants. According to Mayor Alejandro Éder, there are at least 95 dead. Under the scorching heat on Tuesday morning, Torres del Limonar is a shattered mountain of rubble, with mattresses, furniture, and belongings peeking out from the concrete. On top of the remains are rescuers and volunteers: "Silence! We are firefighters. If you can hear us, shout or make any noise." The phrase is repeated every time the teams dig deep enough to believe they may be close to a survivor. These are the moments when Gallego regains hope, but the seconds pass and no answers come from below. Torres del Limonar is one of more than 50 collapsed buildings in Cali. It is located in its south, in the Capri neighbourhood. The four-storey building held dozens of apartments. The exact number of tenants who were inside when it collapsed is unknown. Around it, apart from some cracks, the rest of the buildings seem to have escaped the fate of the Torres. Rescuers, military personnel, volunteers, paramedics, firefighters, humanitarian workers, and journalists have come here. There are more than 100 people waiting for news. According to Mayor Éder, as of Monday night, it was estimated that 25 people were trapped under the rubble. Éder declared a nighttime curfew to speed up rescue operations. The night passed. Excavations continue. A rescuer at the site said about 10 people had been saved since the collapse. Reports in local media, such as one from Blu Pacífico radio, spoke of six survivors up until a few minutes before my arrival, including an infant only a few months old. In the midst of tragedy, figures are often closer to estimates than definitive data. "What I can tell you is that right now there are at least two people detected alive. Tunnels are being made to get them out. One of them has to have his leg freed," rescuer James Velasco tells me. The magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck Colombia on Monday, 10 August, is the worst in this century, according to the National Geological Service. In addition to Cali, it left destruction and death in other regions such as Chocó, in the north-west. Around the remains of Torres del Limonar, unlike Gallego, many residents choose not to speak. They are visibly affected. Some sleep exhausted on the ground or on a sofa placed in the street. Others gather together under the shade for support. The hours are long, increasingly so, and the anguish grows. Velasco offers hope. "In the past I have participated in operations where we have pulled out survivors after seven days trapped." "Those who are meant to survive, survive. Nothing is written," he adds. "I wanted to help from the very beginning." Amid his anguish, Gallego wants to acknowledge the work of ordinary citizens. "We must mention all the people who have come to help with water, supplies, tools, equipment; there is a lot of collaboration. Volunteers are plentiful," he says. Alejandro Mahecha, 19, is one of those volunteers. He decided to come after spending the night safely with his family and overcoming the initial shock. "I wanted to help from the very beginning. The earthquake affected my city and the homes of people I know. I came to this site because there has been a lot of talk about this building and the need for help here," the young man explains. Together with several friends, Mahecha helps remove rubble, bring water to rescuers, and clear the street to facilitate evacuation efforts. In the background, hammers and saws can be heard creating escape routes through the destruction. They stop only when those present raise their arms. That means everyone must remain silent. Gallego waits. This time, too, there was no news of his brother. Related topics - Published6 hours ago

item.title: How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana raft
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye8332d63o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana raft - Published Well past midnight on 19 July, as floodwaters surged through a village in India's northeastern state of Assam, Bornali Baruah and her husband were trying to save his 97-year-old mother. Almost bedridden, Lokada Duarah could not walk. There was no boat, no rescue team and no neighbour available to help. So they lifted her onto a makeshift raft made of banana trunks, and carried her through the rushing water towards safety. "Everyone was trying to save themselves," Baruah says. An hour later, she says, the three of them reached a shelter camp on a national highway some distance away from their house in Charing village in Sivasagar district, one of the worst flood-affected districts. The water was three to four feet deep and the current so strong that they had to move slowly, holding each other's hands and using sticks to steady themselves. By then, Baruah's home was disappearing beneath the flood. The water would eventually rise to about five feet inside it. The scene in Charing was part of a much wider disaster unfolding across Assam. The latest figures put the death toll from floods at 100, with 10 districts and 456 villages affected and about 140,000 people impacted. Fifty-two relief camps have been set up. Overall, the floods have affected nearly 1.2 million people across 25 districts, damaged more than 19,000 houses and left more than 75,000 people in 252 relief camps. The floods have been particularly severe in parts of Upper Assam, where villages like Charing that do not usually flood have been inundated. For Baruah, 40, the shock is especially profound. "This is the first flood we have experienced in this area in our lifetime," she says. Baruah has lived in Charing since birth, and her ancestors lived here before her. She recalls hearing about a major flood in 1950, long before she was born, but nothing like this had happened during her lifetime. Her home sits in a landscape criss-crossed by rivers, though none runs immediately beside it. The single-storey, eight-room house is about 25km (15 miles) from Sivasagar town; the Brahmaputra is roughly 20km away, the Dikhow 12km, the Jhanji 10km and the Mitong just 5km. She had never imagined the water would reach her doorstep. But when it did, the flood threatened not only her home, but the livelihood she had spent years building. Baruah was once a full-time journalist. In 2016, she left the profession to take up animal husbandry, and three years later was named Assam's 'Best Livestock Farmer'. Her farm grew to around 300 goats, 500 ducks and 1,000 chickens, along with fish. The flood destroyed much of it. She says she lost most of her goats, 300 ducks, 300 chickens and a sizeable amount of fish, as well as the machine she used to make animal feed. Furniture, laptops, vehicles and the family's collection of books were also destroyed. None of her livestock was insured. "There is no insurance system here for livestock, especially goats," she says. The first warning came on 17 July, when the Jhanji river began to rise. Two days later, the Dikhow and Mitong spilled into surrounding areas as the Brahmaputra and its tributaries swelled rapidly. Several rivers breached their embankments, Baruah says, sending powerful currents through towns and villages. About a day after the water began rising, she and her family abandoned their home. By then, the water inside the house was four feet deep. They spent the next 10 days in a relief camp. For five days in the camp there was no electricity or mobile connectivity and Baruah could not even charge her phone. The government provided the family with a relief kit containing rice, lentils and cooking oil. Help also came from strangers at the camp. A young woman whom Bornali had never met, helped with food, cleaning and looking after her 60 surviving goats. Another took responsibility for treating and feeding animals that had fallen ill. But why did the water reach a place that Baruah says had never flooded before? Dhrubajyoti Sahariah, a professor of geography and director of the Centre for Brahmaputra Studies at Gauhati University, says flooding itself is natural in the Brahmaputra Valley, a lowland region in Assam. What has changed is the "frequency, intensity and severity of floods well beyond historical norms". The Brahmaputra, one of the world's largest multi-channel rivers, ranks among the top five globally for both water discharge and sediment load. Much of that sediment comes from Tibet, where the river originates. As it enters Assam's vast floodplains, home to some 28 million people and hemmed in by hills, it slows and deposits sediment, fuelling erosion and floods. Flooding is an annual feature of life in Assam, but some years are far worse: the 2004 floods alone affected 12 million people and killed 251. In the recent floods, Sahariah says, continuous heavy rainfall in Upper Assam and neighbouring Nagaland's Mon district triggered severe flooding and large-scale silt deposition in Sivasagar, Charaideo and Jorhat. Sahariah says floods are reaching areas once spared because more people have settled on active floodplains, forests have been cleared, mining and hill-cutting have increased sediment in rivers, and roads, bridges and other infrastructure have been built without adequately accounting for the region's hydrology. Yet Assam cannot manage the Brahmaputra on its own. Many of its tributaries originate in the surrounding hill states, while flood-control measures are largely planned within Assam. "What is needed is basin-scale planning," Sahariah says, along with greater coordination between states and better understanding of the rivers' changing geography. For Baruah, however, the science has become painfully personal. She has returned to the area around her flood-damaged home. For now, she and her family are staying at a neighbour's house nearby, hoping to move back into their own home within a week. Baruah says she does not intend to leave Charing. Moving away, she says, requires economic and social circumstances that her family simply does not have. So she is beginning to think about how to live with a threat that was, until now, largely absent from her life. She says that if heavy rain comes again, she would need to raise the house higher, perhaps by building up its foundation. She is not yet sure how she would manage it or pay for it. The family would also need a raised platform where they could retreat to safety, and they would stock food and drinking water in advance. Baruah is learning to live with the possibility of more floods – and to prepare for them. Did she feel like a climate refugee? "No. If we regain our economic and mental strength, life will return to the way it was before." "We will have to learn to coexist with the floods."

item.title: The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/basketball/articles/ckg3enx6rj6o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA - Published The WNBA is still in the midst of its 2026 season and yet it is next year's Draft for North America's top women's basketball league that is dominating the headlines. Why? Because some former men's NBA players have declared they will enter for selection - citing the current eligibility guidelines, or lack of, for transgender women players. "I'm officially declaring myself a WNBA prospect," said Enes Kanter Freedom, who played 11 seasons in the NBA. It is the latest development in a story ignited by a comment made by Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham, who said she wanted to protect young girls "who shouldn't have to go against biological men" in sport. Her words have instigated protests - albeit not grand in scale - on both sides of the argument, and once again catapulted the debate around transgender women in sport into the spotlight. How did we get here? Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN, external in which the conversation turned to the topic of "protecting" women's sports. The Indiana Fever guard said she had received criticism from people who believed she "hated" transgender people, something she denied. She said she wanted to "extend love" to everyone, but added: "I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men." She later doubled down on her comments, saying it was "common sense", external to bar transgender athletes from competing in women's sports. Her words quickly moved beyond basketball and into a wider political debate in the United States. President Donald Trump expressed his support for Cunningham, while vice-president JD Vance said she was "inspiring". Though the 29-year-old later said she is "not a very political person", her remarks have followed her around the country. Competing rallies from critics and supporters were organised at Indiana's games, along with small-scale protests. The scale of the debate in the media, online and in politics was striking given no openly transgender woman is due to play, or has ever played, in the WNBA. What do the rules say? The WNBA operates under a collective bargaining agreement (CBA), a deal negotiated between the league and its players association (WNBPA), setting rules on matters including player salary caps, revenue sharing, benefits and overall league operations. On player eligibility, the CBA states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." The WNBA has yet to comment publicly on the row since Cunningham's comments but league commissioner Cathy Engelbert reportedly sent a memo to teams last week in which she said the matter would be discussed at an upcoming pre-arranged meeting with team presidents. In the memo, seen by the Associated Press, external, Engelbert said the league would "always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league". She added: "Our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities." However, the lack of detail in the league's eligibility criteria has been brought to light by Kanter Freedom, who finished his playing career with the Boston Celtics in 2022. "If simply declaring who you are is all that's required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," he wrote on Instagram, external. Kanter Freedom, who has previously spoken out about human rights violations in China and Turkey, among other issues, added: "I know my presence on the court will stir up strong opinions. I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices. "I'm simply asking that the current rules be applied equally to everyone - the rules that represent the very values many WNBA players and coaches have publicly advocated for." A day after Kanter Freedom's 'announcement', Royce White - who made three appearances in the NBA as a player and is now a Republican Senate candidate - said he would also declare for the Draft, adding: "I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball." Whether the vagueness of the rules are by design to leave it open to transgender women or a sign of an oversight that genuinely needs tightening up is not clear. BBC Sport has contacted Cunningham's representatives, the WNBA and WNBPA for comment. What has the reaction been? Cunningham's comments have become a flashpoint inside a league which has a long history of player activism on issues including race, gender equality and LGBTQ+ rights. The players' association did not mention Cunningham by name when it eventually addressed the debate. In a statement the WNBPA denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" and reaffirmed its commitment to "justice, equity, diversity and inclusion". It called on fans to report abusive behaviour at games and added that it would continue to have "hard" conversations but it "will not be used as political pawns". There is strong feeling on both sides of the argument. Minnesota Lynx head coach and president Cheryl Reeve, who said: "I come from a space of inclusion. "The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports." Reeve wore a "Trans Kids Belong" T-shirt before Minnesota played Indiana earlier this month and was seen speaking to Cunningham on court before the game. Cunningham later said the pair had exchanged their perspectives and that the conversation ended with "love and respect". Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams said she would welcome a transgender athlete "on my team or against my team, any time". Last month, the WNBA suspended Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton from attending the team's next five home games after an exchange with two fans, who were sat courtside displaying signs thanking Cunningham for "speaking up for girls". Keaton reportedly confronted the teenage fans and admonished them during the game. The Storm have since apologised. As for Cunningham, the attention has increasingly become an unwelcome distraction. Having defended her original comments, she said recently that she now wanted the conversation to return to what was happening on court. "I want to get back to basketball, it's always been about basketball" she said, arguing that the standard of play in the WNBA was being overshadowed by issues away from the game. But that may prove difficult, as pressure grows on the league to clarify exactly who is eligible to play. What are the rules in other sports? In recent years, many governing bodies in sport have amended their rules about the inclusion of transgender athletes at the elite level, moving more towards restrictions. Athletics, cycling and aquatics, for example, have implemented outright bans on transgender women taking part in women's events. In March, it was announced that the women's category of Olympic sports will be limited to biological females from the LA Olympic Games in 2028. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) says eligibility will be determined by a "once-in-a-lifetime" sex test, which would prevent transgender women and those with differences in sexual development (DSD) who have gone through male puberty from competing. In the United States, transgender women and girls are banned from competing in women's sports categories in schools, universities and the grassroots level. That was part of an executive order - titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" - signed by President Trump last year. It does not cover professional sport.
